FSSAI sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri over one water sample from its Goa plant (22 Nov 2026). Bisleri says independent tests cleared its water. What bromate is, and what an 'unsafe sample' legally means, in one minute.

Why the first rain on dry mud smells so good

All summer, oils from plants and an earthy smell made by tiny soil bacteria collect in dry soil. This is called petrichor. A raindrop on soil full of tiny holes traps air bubbles that rise and burst like goli soda fizz, flinging a fine mist into the air - scientists say the smell rides on it. In Kannauj, perfume makers bake this mud into mitti attar.

Which memory does the smell of the first rain bring back for you? 👇

That su-su sound on the Ganga is an almost blind dolphin

The Ganga river dolphin is India's National Aquatic Animal. Its eyes have no lens, so in the muddy river it is almost blind. It finds fish by sending clicks and listening for the echo - this is called echolocation. Its breathing sound gave it the name susu.

Have you ever seen a dolphin in an Indian river? 👇

Why your call drops the moment the lift door shuts

Your phone's signal comes from a tower as radio waves that pass through walls, but a lift is a closed steel box. The wave makes tiny currents in the metal that cancel it - this is called a Faraday cage. The metal mesh on a microwave oven door does the same job.

Where in your home or office does the signal always vanish? 👇

The sea railway bridge that rises like a lift

The new Pamban bridge is India's first vertical-lift railway sea bridge. When a ship comes, its middle steel span rises straight up, flat. Huge counterweights in the towers balance it, just like a building lift, so small electric motors are enough.

Have you ever crossed this bridge by train? 👇

Two Bilaspurs: how your PIN code finds the right one

India has a Bilaspur in Himachal and another in Chhattisgarh, yet letters never mix them up. The six-digit PIN code does it: the first digit is the zone, the second a smaller area, the third the sorting district, and the last digits your own post office.

Why the 800-year-old Ramappa temple stands on sand

The Ramappa temple in Telangana, about 800 years old, stands on a pit filled with sand mixed with lime and jaggery. In an earthquake the sand works like a cushion and soaks up the shake - this is called the sandbox technique. Its tower is said to use bricks light enough to float on water.

The bridge in Meghalaya that is alive

In Meghalaya, Khasi and Jaintia villagers don't build bridges, they grow them. Young roots of a rubber tree are guided across a stream through hollow supari (areca) trunks or over bamboo, and take about fifteen years or more to carry people. In one of the rainiest places on Earth wood rots fast, but living roots fuse, thicken and keep getting stronger as long as the tree lives.

Why the Statue of Unity doesn't fall in strong wind

The Statue of Unity looks like solid bronze, but inside it is a concrete building. Concrete towers rise through the legs to the chest, a steel frame is fixed to them, and outside there are only 8 mm bronze panels that overlap and can move a little in the wind.

How the Army rebuilt Wayanad's lost bridge by next evening

When a landslide flood washed away a bridge in Wayanad, Kerala, the Indian Army's Madras Engineer Group had a 190-foot Bailey bridge carrying vehicles by the next evening. A Bailey bridge is a ready-made steel kit: identical panels joined with steel pins, rolled out over the gap behind a light launching nose, no big crane needed.

Gave blood, won't you get weak? How your body refills it

One bag of donated blood is only about one-tenth of the blood in your body. The watery part, plasma, comes back in about a day or two; red cells take a few weeks. A message from the kidney makes the bone marrow, the soft inside of your bones, run extra shifts to make new red cells.

Have you ever donated blood, and how did you feel that day? 👇

Why an elephant keeps flapping its ears on a hot day

An elephant hardly sweats, but its ears work like a radiator. The paper-thin ear skin is packed with blood vessels; every flap blows air over the warm blood, and the cooler blood flows back into the body - like radiator water going back to a bus engine.

Where is the closest you have ever been to an elephant? 👇

Arrive hungry at the Golden Temple, get fed free. How?

First time at the Golden Temple, Amritsar: a free shoe stand with a token, scarves at the gate, shallow water to wash your feet, a marble walk around the holy pool, then the langar hall where everyone sits on the floor in the same rows. The kitchen runs day and night on sewa (volunteers, many of them visitors) and donations - up to about one lakh meals on big days.

Why the pressure cooker cooks dal so fast

In an open pot, water stops at about 100 degrees. The cooker's lid and rubber gasket trap the steam, the pressure rises and the water gets to about 120 degrees, so dal cooks much faster. Each whistle is the steam lifting the weight and letting out only the extra steam.

Who counts the cooker whistles in your home? 👇

Sabarimala: why police ask for your QR at Pamba

Sabarimala booking is free on the Virtual Queue site (sabarimalaonline.org): pick a date and time slot and get a QR pass. Spot booking is at Nilakkal, Erumeli and Vandiperiyar, not at Pamba. Park at Nilakkal, take the KSRTC bus to Pamba for the QR and Aadhaar check, climb the forest path to the eighteen holy steps (only for irumudi carriers), then aravana (sweet payasam made in the temple's own hilltop plant), appam and free annadanam.
Behind the scenes, everything is planned around the eighteen steps: police keep more than one devotee a second moving, and that pace over a day comes to about 80,000, the daily limit. This is 2026-season information; booking rules change often.

Tirumala darshan with no VIP ticket: where to start

No VIP ticket? Free time-slot token counters in Tirupati, the Rs 300 special entry ticket booked online months ahead, or no token at all - waiting halls in the queue complex with free milk and food, a free laddu after darshan and free meals at the Annaprasadam hall. With over sixty thousand pilgrims a day, the line keeps moving: halls are let out in batches, a control room watches every hall, and the potu kitchen makes over three lakh laddus a day. Token rules change on festival days; check TTD's official site.

Why your fingers go wrinkly in water

After a long time in water your fingertips look like kishmish, but it isn't water soaking in. Your nerves squeeze the tiny blood vessels under the skin, the cushion below shrinks and the tied-down skin folds - a finger with a damaged nerve doesn't wrinkle. Scientists think the ridges may help grip wet things like tyre grooves, though not every study agrees.

Whose fingers in your home go wrinkly the fastest? 👇

Harekala Hajabba sells oranges in Mangaluru and never got to study. Reports say he could not answer a foreign tourist's question about the price of oranges. He saved a little of his small earnings, took loans, bought land and kept asking for help until his village got a school - and received the Padma Shri (2020) barefoot at Rashtrapati Bhavan.

Karimul Haque, a tea-garden worker of Dhalabari in Jalpaiguri, West Bengal, carries sick villagers to hospital on his motorbike for free, day or night - a bike reaches narrow mud roads where an ambulance cannot. Doctors taught him first aid, and in 2017 he received the Padma Shri.

Khashaba Jadhav of Goleshwar, Maharashtra, learned to wrestle on mud. To reach the 1952 Helsinki Olympics, his village chipped in, his college principal mortgaged his house and his coach found more money. He won bronze - independent India's first individual Olympic medal.

The forgotten Indian doctor behind the ORS in every home

Dr Dilip Mahalanabis was a Kolkata children's doctor. In 1971, when cholera spread in the refugee camps near Bangaon and saline drips ran short, his team gave ORS (salt, glucose and baking soda in water) by mouth at huge scale - deaths fell from about 30% to below 4%. He did not invent ORS; the idea came from earlier research, and he proved it at scale. The Lancet called ORS one of the most important medical advances of that century. He was given the Padma Vibhushan after his death (2023).

Had you ever heard his name before today? 👇

Asu, the hand winding of thread round pins for a Pochampally silk saree's design, takes about 9,000 hand movements per saree. Chintakindi Mallesham taught a machine his mother's hand movement and named it Laxmi Asu, after her; he later received the Padma Shri.

April in Ladakh, dry fields, and the engineer who made ice

In Ladakh the big glacier's water arrives only after June, too late for sowing. Civil engineer Chewang Norphel turns a stream into hillside channels in autumn; low stone walls hold it in shallow pools that freeze layer by layer - an artificial glacier. Sitting lower and closer to the village, it melts first, right at sowing time. It earned him the Padma Shri.

She never went to school, now India calls her Seed Mother

Rahibai Popere, a tribal farmer from a Maharashtra village, never went to school, yet she is known as the Seed Mother (Beej Mata). Every harvest she saves the best local seeds, stores them in clay pots with ash sealed with cow dung, and lends them to farmers who return double. Her home seed bank, set up with BAIF, earned her the Padma Shri (2020); she was also on the BBC 100 Women list (2018).

The farmer who grows a tree with one bottle of water

Sundaram Verma, a farmer of Danta village in Sikar, Rajasthan, gives each sapling just one litre of water, once. He ploughs deep after the first rains, removes thirsty weeds, breaks the tiny soil paths that pull water up, and plants in a deep pit, so the roots grow down to the rain stored underground. Cars race over Mumbai's sea: how Atal Setu was built

Atal Setu in Mumbai is India's longest sea bridge. Ships pass above and oil and gas pipelines lie under the seabed, so some gaps between pillars are huge. There the deck is not concrete but a light steel plate with ribs underneath, an orthotropic steel deck. It was made in pieces, joined near the shore, towed out on a huge barge and lifted onto the pillars by jacks.

Midnight, ice and the world's tallest building

As of 2026, Burj Khalifa is still the world's tallest building. In Dubai's heat, wet concrete dries too fast and cracks, so in summer it was poured at night, with ice replacing part of the mixing water. Strong pumps pushed it about 600 m up, a world record back then.

The Maeslant barrier near Rotterdam is part of the Dutch Delta Works. Its giant doors are hollow: empty, they float like a pot; filled with water, they sink and make a wall across the river. After the storm, pumps empty them and they float back to their docks.

At the Panama Canal, giant ships climb water steps called locks up to Gatun Lake, about 26 m above the sea, and come down the other side. There are no pumps: lake water flows down through tunnels in the walls and up through holes in the floor, and the ship floats up.

How engineers saved the falling Tower of Pisa

In 1990 the Leaning Tower of Pisa was shut because it could fall. Engineers did not push it. They drilled under the high north side and took out a little soil at a time, so that side sank and the tower came back about forty centimetres. Lead blocks and steel cables held it safe during the work.

The Godavari floods, yet Polavaram builds its dam in the dry

You cannot stop the Godavari, only move it. So at Polavaram the gated spillway was built first, on dry land beside the river. Then cofferdams pushed the river into it, a diaphragm wall was cut through the sand down to rock, and the earth-and-rock main dam rises on top. As of 2026, that wall is complete.

How giant container ships stop right beside Kerala's coast

At Vizhinjam, the sea is naturally deep right next to the shore, deep enough to swallow a five-storey building. But open-sea waves pound this coast, so engineers built a rock breakwater about three kilometres long: small rocks first, then boulders, then heavy concrete blocks on the wave side. Behind it the water stays calm for giant container ships.

Zojila: the Himalayan road snow shuts for months

Every winter, snow and avalanches shut the Zojila Pass road between Kashmir and Ladakh for months. So engineers are digging a road tunnel of about 13 km through the mountain, from both ends: drill holes, blast, spray concrete at once, add steel ribs. Both ends met in June 2026; the opening target is around 2028. It is said to be one of the longest two-way single-tube road tunnels.

The volcano with cold mud: Baratang, Andaman

On Baratang island in the Andamans, north of Port Blair, there is a volcano with no fire - a mud volcano. Gas from plants and sea life buried and rotting deep underground (mostly methane) builds pressure and pushes cold mud, about 30 degrees, up through cracks in the rock. In October 2025 it erupted big again after about twenty years. The fire-and-lava kind in the same islands is Barren Island. Visuals are AI-made.

Stone icicles in a dark Araku cave: how Borra Caves formed

The Borra Caves in the Ananthagiri hills of Andhra Pradesh's Araku valley are said to go about 80 m deep. Slightly sour rain and Gosthani river water slowly dissolved the soft limestone over ages, and every drip leaves a thin ring of stone behind, growing stone icicles called stalactites. On the Umngot river at Dawki, Meghalaya, wooden boats seem to hang in mid-air. The real reason: in the dry months (roughly November to April) almost no mud washes in, sunlight goes straight to the stony bed, and the boat's own shadow falls on the stones below. The Himachal house that sways but rarely falls: Kath-Kuni

In Kullu, the Shimla hills and Kinnaur, Kath-Kuni houses are built from layers of deodar wood and stone with no cement (kath = wood, kuni = corner). Beams lock at the corners with wooden pins, heavy stone holds the house down and the wood bends, so in an earthquake it sways but rarely falls. Naggar Castle in Kullu came through the 1905 earthquake. Visuals are AI-made.

80 feet down, water flows with no pump: Kundi Bhandara

Kundi Bhandara in Burhanpur, Madhya Pradesh, on the Tapti river, was built in Mughal times about four hundred years ago. Rain that soaks into the Satpura hills is caught by a tunnel dug into the slope and flows downhill to the city with no pump and no electricity; round wells called kundis let air in and give workers a way down to clean it. The crater lake in Maharashtra that turned pink: Lonar

Lonar Lake in Buldhana, Maharashtra, sits in a bowl made thousands of years ago when a meteorite hit the hard black basalt of the Deccan. With no way out, its water is salty and alkaline, a bit like washing-soda water. In the hot, dry summer of 2020 the water dropped and got saltier, and tiny salt-loving microbes turned the lake pink (tested by labs in Pune and Nagpur). Visuals are AI-made.

A wall in his house hid a city underground: Derinkuyu

The story goes, in 1963 a man in Turkey broke a wall in his house and found Derinkuyu, a whole city under the ground. People carved it floor below floor into tuff, a soft rock made of volcanic ash; air shafts brought fresh air down, deep wells gave water, and round millstone-like stone doors rolled shut from inside. India's own Kailasa temple at Ellora was carved from one single rock, top down.

How Easter Island's giant statues walked

Easter Island (Rapa Nui) has almost a thousand stone statues called moai, and the islanders' old story says they walked. Researchers showed they were moved standing up, rocked side to side with ropes so they "walked" - helped by their forward lean, wide rounded bases and roads dipped in the middle. In a test, eighteen people walked a replica.

Why Dubai's sand island Palm Jumeirah does not wash away

Palm Jumeirah has no concrete base under it, just sand from the sea bed and rock. A crescent rock wall about eleven kilometres long stops the waves, dredger ships sprayed the sand into the palm shape guided by satellites, and long vibrating rods shook the sand tight. Mumbai too was once seven islands, joined by filling the sea.

How Japan's bullet train beats an earthquake
